q: A CA files for a monthly client. In what order do the main steps happen each month?
options: Collect sales data and file GSTR-1 (by the 11th), act on IMS and check GSTR-2B (from the 14th), reconcile purchases, then pay tax and file GSTR-3B (by the 20th)
Reconcile once a year, file GSTR-9, then monthly returns
Pay tax first, then file everything on the 20th
exp: GSTR-1 comes first because GSTR-3B liability is auto-populated from it and 3B can't be filed until GSTR-1 is. Purchases are reconciled against 2B before claiming ITC.

q: On the 18th, a CA sees ₹6 lakh of the client's purchase invoices are in the books but missing from GSTR-2B. What should go into this month's GSTR-3B?
options: Claim all of it, the invoices are genuine
Claim only what's in GSTR-2B; follow up with those suppliers and claim the rest in the month it appears in 2B
Skip claiming ITC this month altogether
exp: Section 16(2)(aa) and rule 36(4) restrict ITC to what's in 2B. Claiming more also triggers a rule 88D intimation. The missed ITC isn't lost; it can be claimed later within the section 16(4) deadline.

q: A client's GSTR-3B shows ₹3 lakh output tax and ₹2.2 lakh ITC. Its cash ledger has ₹50,000. What does the CA do before filing?
options: File anyway, the portal will adjust
Create a PMT-06 challan for the ₹30,000 shortfall, get the client to pay, then offset liability and file
Claim more ITC to cover it
File a nil return and pay later
exp: GSTR-3B can only be filed once liability is fully offset. Net cash needed is ₹80,000; with ₹50,000 in the ledger, ₹30,000 more must be deposited.

q: A client with ₹3 crore turnover asks whether to switch to QRMP. What's the main trade-off the CA should explain?
options: Returns become quarterly but tax is still paid monthly (PMT-06); B2B buyers may want IFF uploads so their ITC isn't delayed
QRMP removes the need for GSTR-1
QRMP has a lower tax rate
exp: QRMP reduces filing effort, but monthly payments continue and B2B clients' ITC depends on when invoices are uploaded.

q: In IMS, a client's supplier has uploaded an invoice for goods that haven't arrived yet. What's the right action this month?
options: Keep it Pending so it doesn't enter this month's 2B, and accept it once goods are received
exp: ITC needs actual receipt of goods (s.16(2)(b)). Pending defers it. Ignoring means it's deemed accepted.

q: A CA notices a client's biggest supplier hasn't filed GSTR-1 for two months. What's the most useful advice to the client?
options: Hold part of the payment until the supplier files, since the client can't claim that ITC and may have to reverse it if the supplier never pays the tax
Report the supplier to the police
exp: Vendor compliance directly affects the buyer's ITC. Many clients add clauses allowing them to withhold GST amounts until invoices reflect in 2B.

q: At year end a CA prepares GSTR-9 for a client. Where do the figures mostly come from?
options: Auto-populated from the year's GSTR-1, GSTR-3B and GSTR-2B, then checked against books; differences are explained or paid through DRC-03
exp: GSTR-9 isn't a chance to revise earlier returns. It reports the year as filed, and extra liability found is paid via DRC-03.

q: You've just taken on a new trading client in Delhi who files monthly. Walk through what you'd set up and check in the first week.
model: Get the GSTIN, portal login, and the authorised signatory's mobile for EVC OTPs (or DSC if it's a company or LLP). Check the portal for filing status of past returns, any notices under 'View notices and orders' and the additional notices tab, and the cash and credit ledger balances. Enrol as the client's GST practitioner if you'll be filing on their behalf. Agree a monthly calendar: sales data by around the 5th for GSTR-1 on the 11th, purchase data before the 14th for 2B reconciliation, and payment before the 20th. Check whether e-invoicing applies (turnover above ₹5 crore in any year) and whether HSN digits on invoices are right.
points: Past filing status and pending notices
exp: Most compliance failures come from data arriving late, not from not knowing the law.

q: A client's GSTR-3B for August is filed on 5 October instead of 20 September. What does the client owe on top of the tax?
options: Late fee per day of delay (subject to a cap) plus 18% interest on the tax paid in cash, for the days of delay
Only interest on the full liability
exp: Late fee under s.47 and interest under s.50 on the net cash portion. Both are paid in cash before filing.

q: A client missed filing GSTR-1 for July and it's now 18 August. What else is affected?
options: July's GSTR-3B can't be filed until July's GSTR-1 is filed, and the client's B2B buyers won't see the invoices in their July 2B
exp: Section 39(10) links the two. Buyers get the ITC only in the 2B of the month the invoices are eventually filed.

q: A client hasn't filed GSTR-3B for two consecutive months. What operational problem hits first?
options: E-way bill generation gets blocked for the GSTIN, which can stop dispatches
exp: Rule 138E. For a trading or manufacturing client this stops trucks leaving, which is usually what makes them call.

q: A non-filer client receives a GSTR-3A notice. What is it?
options: A notice to file the pending return within 15 days, before the officer can do a best judgement assessment
exp: If the return still isn't filed, the officer may assess under s.62 (ASMT-13). That order is withdrawn if the return is filed within 60 days.

q: A client hasn't filed returns for six months straight. What's the risk?
options: The officer can start cancellation of registration (REG-17 show cause notice)
exp: Section 29(2)(c) allows cancellation for non-filing over a continuous period. Once cancelled, the client can't issue tax invoices.

q: A client wants to file an old GSTR-3B from more than three years ago. What will happen?
options: The portal won't accept it, returns are time-barred three years after their due date
exp: Enforced from July 2025. Any tax still due gets settled through DRC-03 or proceedings, not a return.

q: A client files GSTR-3B late with a nil liability. Is there a late fee?
options: No, nil returns have no late fee
Yes, a reduced late fee per day applies to nil returns, subject to a cap
Only if more than 90 days late
exp: Nil returns carry a lower per-day fee but aren't free. They can be filed by SMS.

q: A client's supplier invoice dated June 2024 appears in 2B only in December 2025 because the supplier filed very late. Can the client claim that ITC now?
options: No, the section 16(4) deadline for FY 2024-25 invoices was 30 November 2025
exp: This is why chasing suppliers before 30 November matters. The ITC is lost if it doesn't reach 2B in time.

q: A client calls on 22nd evening: 'I forgot to send you data, GSTR-3B was due on the 20th.' What do you tell them and what do you do?
model: Reassure them it's fixable. File GSTR-1 first if it's pending, since 3B depends on it. Prepare 3B as soon as data arrives. Late fee accrues per day, so each day counts, and interest at 18% runs on the tax paid in cash from the 21st. Pay both through the cash ledger before filing. If two consecutive 3Bs go unfiled, e-way bills get blocked, so file this before next month's due date. Then fix the process: agree a data cut-off date and send reminders.
points: Late fee per day plus 18% interest on cash tax
Pay through cash ledger before filing
Watch the two-period e-way bill block
exp: CAs deal with this constantly. The skill is minimising the damage quickly.

q: A CA realises an invoice was reported with the wrong taxable value in last month's GSTR-1, already filed. How is it corrected?
options: Amend it in the current or a later GSTR-1 using the amendment table (9A), since filed returns can't be revised
exp: There's no revision of filed GST returns. Amendments are made in later returns within the section 37(3) time limit.

q: What's the last date to amend errors in FY 2024-25 GSTR-1 details?
options: 30 November 2025, or the date the annual return is filed if earlier
exp: The same time limit applies to rectifying GSTR-3B under s.39(9).

q: A client's B2B invoice went out under the wrong buyer GSTIN in GSTR-1. The buyer complains the ITC isn't showing. What's the fix?
options: Amend the invoice in the next GSTR-1 (Table 9A) with the correct GSTIN, so it moves to the right buyer's 2B
Issue a new invoice with a new number
exp: The wrongly named recipient may have seen it in their 2B, which is why their team may also flag it.

q: A CA spots the error before filing GSTR-3B but after filing GSTR-1 for the same month. What's the quickest correction?
options: Use GSTR-1A for that month, so the corrected figures auto-populate this month's GSTR-3B
exp: GSTR-1A exists exactly for this window.

q: A client under-reported ₹2 lakh of output tax in April's GSTR-3B. It's now July. How is it fixed?
options: Add the ₹2 lakh to July's GSTR-3B (or pay through DRC-03) with interest from April's due date
exp: Additional liability is declared in a later return with interest calculated from the original due date.

q: A client forgot to claim eligible ITC of ₹80,000 in May's GSTR-3B, though it was in May's 2B. Can it be claimed in August?
options: Yes, in a later 3B's Table 4(A)(5), within the section 16(4) time limit
exp: ITC isn't lost for being claimed late, as long as it's within the time limit.

q: A client paid IGST on a sale that should have been CGST+SGST. The tax amount is the same. What's the correct fix?
options: Pay CGST+SGST correctly, then claim a refund of the IGST paid under section 77/19
Transfer IGST to CGST using PMT-09
exp: Wrong-head tax can't simply be moved once it's discharged in a return. The refund is claimed within two years of paying the correct tax.
ref: CGST Act, s.77; IGST Act, s.19

q: A CA over-reported liability by ₹50,000 in GSTR-3B for a month, and it's been paid. What are the options?
options: Reduce liability in a later GSTR-3B (where the portal allows), or claim a refund of excess tax paid
exp: Excess payment can be adjusted in later returns within limits or refunded under s.54. With auto-populated liability now locked, most corrections start at GSTR-1 or GSTR-1A.

q: While preparing GSTR-9, a CA finds ₹1.2 lakh of tax that was never paid during the year. How is it settled?
options: Pay it through DRC-03 with interest, and report it in GSTR-9
Ignore it, the year is closed
Pay in next year's GSTR-3B with no interest
exp: GSTR-9 itself can't be used to pay tax. DRC-03 is the voluntary payment form.

q: A client issued an invoice of ₹5 lakh + ₹90,000 IGST to a customer, reported it in GSTR-1 and paid the tax. Two months later, the customer says half the goods were defective and returns them. What should the CA do?
model: Issue a GST credit note for the returned half (₹2.5 lakh + ₹45,000 IGST), referencing the original invoice, and report it in GSTR-1 Table 9B. If the client is on e-invoicing, register the credit note on the IRP. The supplier's liability reduces in the month the credit note is reported, subject to the customer accepting it in IMS (a rejected credit note won't reduce liability). The customer reverses the matching ITC. This must happen by 30 November after the FY of the original supply.
points: Credit note, not a revised invoice
Report in GSTR-1 Table 9B, and on the IRP if applicable
exp: Returns of goods are the most common reason for credit notes.

q: Where does a CA check whether a client has received any GST notice?
options: On the GST portal under Services > User Services > View Notices and Orders, and also the Additional Notices and Orders tab
exp: Notices uploaded on the portal count as valid service under section 169. Missing the Additional Notices tab is a common, expensive mistake.

q: A client receives ASMT-10 saying GSTR-3B ITC is higher than GSTR-2B. How is it answered?
options: Reply in ASMT-11 within the time given (usually 30 days), with a reconciliation explaining the difference or accepting and paying through DRC-03
exp: If the officer accepts the reply, ASMT-12 closes it. If not, it can lead to a demand under s.73/74 (or 74A for FY 2024-25 onwards).

q: A client gets DRC-01B saying GSTR-1 liability exceeds GSTR-3B. What's the deadline and consequence?
options: Reply in Part B within 7 days, paying the difference or explaining it; otherwise the next GSTR-1 is blocked
exp: The explanation might be that invoices were reported in GSTR-1 but tax was paid in a different month.

q: A client receives a show cause notice (DRC-01) for FY 2022-23 under section 73 demanding ₹4 lakh. If the client agrees with the demand, what's the cheapest option?
options: Pay the tax and interest within 30 days of the SCN, which means no penalty under section 73
exp: Under s.73(8) no penalty applies if tax and interest are paid within 30 days of the notice.

q: A demand relates to FY 2024-25. Which section governs it?
options: Section 74A, the single section for all demands from FY 2024-25 onwards
exp: 74A merged the fraud and non-fraud routes, with a common time limit of 42 months from the annual return due date for the notice.

q: A client disagrees with a demand order (DRC-07). What must happen within three months?
options: File an appeal before the Appellate Authority (APL-01) with a pre-deposit of 10% of the disputed tax
exp: The pre-deposit stops recovery of the balance while the appeal is pending. A further appeal goes to the GSTAT.

q: A client's cancellation show cause notice (REG-17) arrives for non-filing. What should the CA do?
options: File the pending returns with late fee and interest, and reply in REG-18 within the time allowed (7 working days)
exp: If the registration is cancelled anyway, a revocation application (REG-21) can be filed within the allowed time after filing pending returns.

q: The officer blocks a client's electronic credit ledger under rule 86A without any notice. What should the CA know?
options: Blocking can happen without prior notice, lasts up to one year, and the client can make a representation; courts have required reasons to be recorded
Only the court can block it
It can be undone by filing GSTR-9
exp: Many writ petitions have been filed on this. Blocked credit can't be used for payment or refund.

q: A client is issued summons under section 70. What is it?
options: A direction to appear and give evidence or produce documents in an inquiry
A notice to file a return
exp: Summons is part of an investigation, not an assessment. Ignoring it can lead to penalties.

q: A client receives an ASMT-10 for FY 2020-21: ITC in GSTR-3B is ₹4.2 lakh more than GSTR-2A. The client says every invoice is genuine. How would you draft the reply?
model: Reply in ASMT-11 within the deadline. Attach an invoice-wise reconciliation of the ₹4.2 lakh gap: invoices where suppliers filed late (show them in later 2A), wrong GSTIN or period reported by suppliers, and IGST on imports from ICEGATE that doesn't appear in 2A. For this period, cite Circular 183/15/2022 as extended by Circular 193/05/2023 (covering April 2019 to December 2021), which lets a buyer prove genuine credit with a supplier's CA certificate (above ₹5 lakh) or supplier certificate (up to ₹5 lakh) that tax was paid. Attach invoices, payment proof and e-way bills. Pay through DRC-03 only for anything genuinely ineligible, so the rest isn't conceded.
points: Payment only for truly ineligible amounts
exp: 2A-vs-3B notices for old years are among the most common notices CAs handle.

q: A client ignored a show cause notice and now has a demand order of ₹12 lakh (tax ₹8 lakh, interest and penalty the rest). Their bank account has just been attached. What are the options?
model: The order can still be appealed within three months (plus one month on sufficient cause) under section 107. Paying the 10% pre-deposit (₹80,000 on disputed tax) with the appeal stays recovery of the balance, and the CA can ask the officer to lift the attachment once the appeal is filed. If the appeal deadline has passed, a writ petition in the High Court is the remaining route, usually only where there's a breach of natural justice. For the future: check the portal notices section regularly.
points: Stay of recovery on filing the appeal
Writ if the appeal window closed
exp: Most bank attachments CAs see come from missed portal notices.

q: A private limited company client needs its GSTR-3B filed. How is it signed?
options: EVC OTP on the CA's mobile
DSC of the authorised signatory registered on the portal
exp: Companies and LLPs must use DSC. Other taxpayers can use EVC, with the OTP going to the authorised signatory's mobile.

q: What does a CA's enrolment as a GST Practitioner (GSTP) allow on the portal?
options: Preparing and furnishing returns and other forms on the client's behalf once the client authorises the GSTP, with the client confirming
exp: The taxpayer remains responsible for what's filed.

q: A proprietor client's authorised signatory mobile number is lost, so EVC OTPs aren't coming. What's the fix?
options: Update the authorised signatory's contact details through a non-core amendment (with email/mobile OTP and verification steps), then file
exp: Keeping authorised signatory details current avoids a scramble at due dates.

q: A client asks the CA to 'just show some purchase bills' to increase ITC. What's the right response?
options: Refuse; claiming ITC on fake invoices is an offence under section 132 with penalties and possible arrest
exp: Fake invoice ITC is one of the department's main enforcement targets, and a professional helping with it is also exposed.

q: You manage 60 GST clients. What would you want from a GST compliance software to make the monthly cycle manageable?
model: A dashboard of every client's filing status and due dates, with pending data flagged. Bulk GSTR-1 preparation from sales data or e-invoices. Automatic 2B download and reconciliation with the purchase register, with IMS actions done in bulk. A vendor follow-up list for missing invoices. Payment computation and challan creation. Alerts for new portal notices, rule 88C/88D intimations and e-way bill blocking risk. Audit trails of who filed what. This is essentially the product surface a GST SaaS company builds for CAs.
points: Bulk GSTR-1 from sales or e-invoices
exp: Thinking from the CA's side is the fastest way to understand why each feature exists.
